Error-Handling Middleware →

The asyncHandler Wrapper

A closure that catches a rejected Promise from your controller and hands it to Express properly.

Figure 1.9 is the entire asyncHandler — small, but worth reading slowly with the closures topic from earlier in this lesson, and the previous slide's Express-specific async gap, both fresh:

// Figure 1.9: catching async errors (src/middleware/asyncHandler.js)
export default (fn) => (req, res, next) => {
  Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);
};

This is precisely the (a) => (b) => ... shape from the arrow-functions refresher. asyncHandler is called once per controller with the real controller function as fn — look back at Figure 1.7: asyncHandler(async (req, res) => { ... }). That call returns a new function, closing over fn, and that new function is what Express actually calls as the route handler.

Inside it: fn(req, res, next) runs your controller and gets back a Promise (every async function returns one, previous slide). Promise.resolve(...) is a safety net — it works even if fn weren't async and returned a plain value. .catch(next) is the whole point: if that Promise rejects, next (the real Express next function, passed through) gets called with the error.

Calling next(someError) is Express's own signal to skip every remaining normal middleware and jump straight to error-handling middleware — the next slide. So the fix for "Express never awaits your handler" isn't awaiting it after all; it's routing the rejection to next() by hand, which Express does know how to act on.
